title: Estius states the same and raises against himself the objection from freedom
source_text: XXII. Atque his consentanea sunt quae leguntur apud Estium loco supra citato, ubi exposita eadem sententia, & multis in illius confirmationem adductis, sic concludit, & adversus voluntatis humanae libertatem sibi objicit, Cum igitur ex dictis pateat voluntatem nostram ad actiones suas efficaciter moveri & determinari a Deo tanquam prima causa, primoque agente, movente, deliberante, & proinde ab eo praeveniri ac praedeterminari, restat explicandum quomodo cum efficaci illa motione, ac determinatione, imo praemotione ac praedeterminatione divina, consistat libertas voluntatis nostrae. Non enim videtur relinqui liberum ad utrumlibet id quod a priori causa efficaciter movetur & determinatur in alteram partem.
pass_a_gloss: And agreeable to these are the things which are read in Estius in the place cited above, where having set forth the same opinion, and adduced many things in its confirmation, he concludes thus, and objects to himself against the liberty of the human will, Since therefore it is plain from what has been said that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as the first cause, and first agent, mover, deliberator, and accordingly is prevented and predetermined by him, it remains to be explained how with that efficacious motion, and determination, nay divine premotion and predetermination, the liberty of our will consists. For that does not seem to be left free to either side which is efficaciously moved and determined by a prior cause to one part.
pass_b_english: What Estius writes in the passage cited above agrees with this. Having set out the same view and brought many arguments to support it, he concludes as follows and raises against himself the objection from the freedom of the human will:

'Since, then, what has been said makes it clear that our will is efficaciously moved and determined to its actions by God as first cause, first agent, mover and deliberator, and is therefore anticipated and predetermined by him, it remains to explain how the freedom of our will is consistent with that efficacious motion and determination, indeed with divine premotion and predetermination. For what a prior cause efficaciously moves and determines to one side does not seem to be left free to go either way.'

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
